Surah al-Saff is Madinan according to the consensus, as mentioned by al-Mawardi. It has been said that it is Makki, as reported by al-Nahhas from Ibn Abbas. It has fourteen verses.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (*al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran*) on Surah 61, verses 2–3:**

There are five issues in this passage.

**The first issue:** God's words, ﴿O you who have believed, why do you say what you do not do?﴾

Al-Darimi Abu Muhammad related in his *Musnad*: Muhammad ibn Kathir informed us, from al-Awza'i, from Yahya ibn Abi Kathir, from Abu Salama, from Abdullah ibn Salam, who said: "A group of us, among the Companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), sat together and discussed. We said, 'If we knew which deeds are most beloved to God, we would perform them.' So God revealed: ﴿Whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth glorifies God, and He is the Mighty, the Wise. O you who have believed, why do you say what you do not do?﴾ up to the end of the surah." Abdullah said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) recited it to us until he finished it." Abu Salama said: "Ibn Salam recited it to us." Yahya said: "Abu Salama recited it to us, and Yahya recited it to us, and al-Awza'i recited it to us, and Muhammad recited it to us."

[[This hadith is as it appears in the *Musnad* of al-Darimi. It is mentioned in the principal sources with irregularity (*mudtarib*).]]

Ibn Abbas said: Abdullah ibn Rawaha said, "If we knew the deeds most beloved to God, we would perform them." But when jihad was prescribed, they disliked it.

Al-Kalbi said: The believers said, "O Messenger of God, if we knew the deeds most beloved to God, we would hasten to them." Then this was revealed: ﴿Shall I direct you to a commerce that will save you from a painful punishment?﴾ [al-Saff: 10]

[[See p. 87 of this surah.]]

They remained for a time saying, "If we knew what it is, we would buy it with our wealth, our selves and our families." So God directed them to it by saying: ﴿You believe in God and His Messenger, and strive in the cause of God with your wealth and your selves﴾ [al-Saff: 11], and so on in the verse. Then they were tested on the day of Uhud and fled, so this was revealed to rebuke them for not fulfilling their promise.

Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: When God informed His Prophet (ﷺ) of the reward of the martyrs of Badr, the Companions said, "O God, bear witness! If we encounter battle, we will expend our utmost effort in it." Then they fled on the day of Uhud, and God rebuked them for that.

Qatadah and al-Dahhak said: It was revealed concerning a people who used to say, "We have struggled and displayed valour," when they had not done so.

Suhayb said: A man had harmed the Muslims on the day of Badr and inflicted wounds on them, so I killed him. Then a man said, "O Prophet of God, I killed so-and-so." The Prophet (ﷺ) was pleased by this. Umar ibn al-Khattab and Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf said, "O Suhayb, did you not tell the Messenger of God (ﷺ) that you had killed so-and-so? For so-and-so claimed the killing." So he informed him, and he said: "Is it so, O Abu Yahya?" He said, "Yes, by God, O Messenger of God." Then the verse was revealed concerning the one who claimed the killing falsely.

Ibn Zayd said: It was revealed concerning the hypocrites, who used to say to the Prophet (ﷺ) and his Companions, "If you go out and fight, we will go out with you and fight." But when they went out, they withdrew from them and held back.

**The second issue:** This verse obliges everyone who binds himself to an act of obedience to fulfil it. In the *Sahih* of Muslim, from Abu Musa, that he sent for the reciters of the people of Basra, and three hundred men who had memorised the Qur'an came to him. He said: "You are the best of the people of Basra and their reciters. Recite it, and let not the lengthy period (of time) weigh upon you, lest your hearts harden as the hearts of those before you hardened. We used to recite a surah which we likened in length and severity to *Bara'a* (al-Tawba), but it was made to be forgotten by us, except that I have preserved from it: 'If the son of Adam had two valleys of wealth, he would seek a third valley; and nothing fills the belly of the son of Adam but dust.'" And we used to recite a surah which we likened to one of the *musabbihat* (surahs beginning with glorifying God), but it was made to be forgotten by us, except that I have preserved from it: "O you who have believed, why do you say what you do not do? Testimony will be written on your necks, and you will be questioned about it on the Day of Resurrection."

Ibn al-Arabi said: All of this is established in the religion. As for the words of God, ﴿O you who have believed, why do you say what you do not do?﴾, it is established in the religion both in wording and meaning in this surah. As for the statement, "Testimony will be written on your necks, and you will be questioned about it on the Day of Resurrection," its meaning is established in the religion, for whoever binds himself to something, it becomes binding upon him by the Law (*shar'*). The thing one binds oneself to is of two kinds. The first is the *nadhr* (vow), which is of two types: a vow of voluntary devotion (*nadhr taqarrub mubtada'*), such as saying, "For God is upon me a prayer, a fast, or a charity," and similar acts of worship. The fulfilment of this is binding by consensus (*ijma'*).

The second is a permissible vow (*nadhr mubah*), which is tied to a condition of desire, such as saying, "If my absent one returns, then upon me is a charity," or tied to a condition of fear, such as saying, "If God spares me the evil of such-and-such, then upon me is a charity." The scholars differed concerning it. Malik and Abu Hanifa said that fulfilling it is binding. Al-Shafi'i, in one of his opinions, said that fulfilling it is not binding.

The generality of the verse is a proof for us, because in its unrestricted form it encompasses the censure of one who says what he does not do, in whatever manner it is said, whether absolute or restricted by a condition. The followers of al-Shafi'i have said that a vow is only valid when its purpose is devotion, and it must be of the kind of devotion. This (type of vow), although it is of the kind of devotion, is not intended for devotion; rather, it is intended to restrain oneself from an act or to undertake an act. We reply: The lawful acts of devotion are burdens and obligations, even though they are acts of devotion. This binding of oneself to this devotion with hardship, in order to bring about a benefit or to avert a harm, does not depart from the ways of religious obligation, nor does it cease to be intended as a means of drawing near (to God).

Ibn al-Arabi said: If what is pledged is a promise, it is either tied to a cause, such as saying, "If you marry, I will assist you with a dinar," or "If you buy such-and-such a need, I will give you such-and-such." This is binding by consensus among the jurists. If it is a bare promise, it has been said that it becomes binding by its being attached (*ta'alluq*) [in Ibn al-Arabi: "by its unrestricted form"]. They have relied on the occasion of revelation of the verse, for it is narrated that they used to say, "If we knew which deed is best or most beloved to God, we would perform it," and so God revealed this verse. This is a hadith with no objection. It is also narrated from Mujahid that when Abdullah ibn Rawaha heard it, he said, "I shall not cease to be confined in the cause of God until I am killed." My own view is that a promise must be fulfilled in every case, except where there is an excuse.

I say: Malik said: As for a mere promise, such as when a man asks another to give him a gift, and the other says to him, "Yes," then it becomes apparent to him that he will not do it, I do not think this is binding on him. Ibn al-Qasim said: If one promises creditors and says, "I call you to witness that I have granted to him what he owes you," this is binding on him. But if he says, "Yes, I will do it," and then it becomes apparent to him (that he will not), I do not think it is binding on him. I say: That is, he is not judged to be bound by it. But as for the noble character and good manliness, yes (it is commendable). God has praised those who keep their promise and fulfil their vow, saying: ﴿And those who fulfil their covenant when they make it﴾ [al-Baqara: 177] [[See vol. 2, p. 239]], and God said: ﴿And mention in the Book Isma'il; indeed he was true to his promise﴾ [Maryam: 54], and its explanation has already passed [[See vol. 11, p. 114]].

**The third issue:** Al-Nakha'i said: "Three verses have prevented me from admonishing the people: ﴿Do you order the people to righteousness and forget yourselves?﴾ [al-Baqara: 44] [[See vol. 1, p. 365]]; ﴿And I do not intend to oppose you in that which I forbid you﴾ [Hud: 88] [[See vol. 9, p. 89]]; and ﴿O you who have believed, why do you say what you do not do?﴾."

Abu Nu'aym al-Hafiz transmitted from the hadith of Malik ibn Dinar, from Thumama, that Anas ibn Malik said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "On the night I was taken on the Night Journey, I passed by a people whose lips were being cut with scissors of fire. Whenever they were cut, they were restored." I said: "Who are these, O Jibril?" He said: "These are the orators of your community who say what they do not do, and who recite the Book of God but do not act upon it." [Note: *wafat* means completed and lengthened.]

It is also related from one of the early pious predecessors (*salaf*) that he was asked, "Speak to us," and he remained silent. Then he was asked again, "Speak to us." He said, "Do you want me to say what I do not do, and thus hasten the hatred of God?"

**The fourth issue:** God's words, ﴿Why do you say what you do not do?﴾, are a question in the form of denunciation and rebuke, that a person should say about himself of goodness what he does not do. As for the past, it is a lie; as for the future, it is a breach of promise. Both are blameworthy.

Sufyan ibn Uyayna interpreted God's words, ﴿Why do you say what you do not do?﴾, to mean: "Why do you say what is not in your power, so that you do not know whether you will do it or not?" According to this, the statement is taken in its apparent sense as a denunciation of (such) speech.

**The fifth issue (marginal):** God's words, ﴿It is greatly hateful in the sight of God that you say what you do not do﴾. This may be cited as evidence for the obligation to fulfil (a vow) made in contention or anger, according to one of al-Shafi'i's two opinions. *Anna* (that) occurs at the beginning of the sentence, and what precedes it is the predicate; it is as if he said: "Your saying what you do not do is blameworthy." It is also permissible that it is the predicate of an omitted subject.

Al-Kisa'i said: *Anna* is in the nominative position, because *kabura* (it is great) is a verb functioning like *bi'sa* (how evil), as in "How evil is a man, your brother." *Maqtan* is in the accusative as a specification (*tamyiz*); the meaning is, "Their saying what they do not do is great in hatefulness." It has also been said that it is a circumstantial accusative (*hal*). *Al-maqt* and *al-maqata* are both verbal nouns (*masdar*). One says *rajul maqit* and *mamqut* when people do not love him.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 61, verse 4:

There are three issues here.

The first: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah loves those who fight in His cause in a row (saff)﴾. That is, they arrange themselves in a row (yasuffūna saffan). The object is implied, meaning they arrange themselves in a row.

(﴿as if they were a structure joined firmly﴾) Al-Farra' said: "marsūs" means "fastened with lead" (bi-l-rasas). Al-Mubarrad said: it is from rassaṣtu al-binā', when I joined its parts together and brought them close until it becomes like a single piece. It was also said: it is from al-rasīs, which is the joining of teeth one to another. And al-tarāṣṣ is mutual adhesion, and from it comes "wa-tarāṣṣū fī al-ṣaff" (and stand firm, closely joined, in the row). The meaning of the verse is: Allah loves the one who stands firm in jihad in the cause of Allah and keeps his place, like the firmness of a building. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: this is an instruction from Allah, exalted is He, to the believers on how they should be when fighting their enemy.

The second: Some of the interpreters (ahl al-ta'wil) have used this verse to argue that fighting on foot is superior to fighting on horseback, because horsemen do not line up in this manner. Al-Mahdawi said: this is not sound, because of what has come concerning the excellence of the horseman in reward and spoils. Horsemen are not excluded from the meaning of the verse, because its meaning is steadfastness.

The third: It is not permissible to leave the row except for a need that arises for a person, or for a message that the imam sends, or for a benefit that appears in the situation, such as an opportunity that is seized, and there is no disagreement about these. Regarding leaving the row for single combat (mubarazah), there is a disagreement on two views. One of them: there is no harm in that, to strike terror into the enemy, to seek martyrdom, and to encourage fighting. Our companions (aṣḥābunā) said: no one should come forward seeking it, because it involves showing off (riya') and going out to what Allah has forbidden, namely meeting the enemy (in such a way). Single combat is only permissible when the disbeliever seeks it, as it occurred in the wars of the Prophet (ﷺ) on the day of Badr and in the expedition of Khaybar, and this is the path the early generations (al-salaf) followed. The matter has already been discussed fully in "al-Baqarah" at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not throw yourselves into destruction with your own hands﴾ [al-Baqarah: 195]. [[See vol. 2, p. (361)]]

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (*al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran*) on surah 61, verse 5:**

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿And when Moses said to his people﴾. When He mentioned the matter of *jihad* (striving in God's cause), He made clear that Moses and Jesus both commanded *tawhid* (affirming God's oneness) and strove in God's cause, and that punishment befell those who opposed them. That is, "And recount to your people, O Muhammad, this story."

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿O my people, why do you hurt me﴾. This was when they accused him of having the *udrah* (a swelling of the testicles), as was mentioned earlier at the end of surah *al-Ahzab* [[see vol. 14, p. (250)]]. Among the harm was what is mentioned in the story of Qarun: that he secretly sent a woman to accuse Moses of fornication.

Among the harm was also their saying: ﴿Make for us a god just as they have gods﴾ [al-A'raf: 138], and their saying: ﴿So go, you and your Lord, and fight [[see vol. 6, p. (812)]]﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 24]. And their saying: "You killed Harun." This has already been mentioned [[see vol. 7, p. 294]].

(﴿And you certainly know that I am the messenger of God to you﴾). The messenger is to be respected and honored. The particle *qad* was added to *ta'lamuna* (you know) for emphasis, as if he had said: "And you know with certain knowledge, with no doubt on your part concerning it."

(﴿So when they deviated﴾), that is, they inclined away from the truth, (﴿God caused their hearts to deviate﴾), that is, He turned their hearts away from guidance. It was also said: "When they deviated from obedience, God caused their hearts to deviate from guidance."

It was also said: "When they deviated from faith, God caused their hearts to deviate from reward." It was also said: that is, when they abandoned what they were commanded regarding honoring the Messenger, peace be upon him, and obeying the Lord, God created misguidance in their hearts as a punishment for their deed.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 61, verse 6:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And when Jesus, son of Mary, said﴾, meaning: and recount to them this account as well. And he said: "O Children of Israel," and he did not say "O my people" as Musa said, because he had no lineage among them that would make them his people.

(﴿Indeed, I am the Messenger of Allah to you﴾), meaning: with the Injil (Gospel).

(﴿confirming what came before me of the Torah﴾) because my description is in the Torah, and because I have not come to you with anything that contradicts the Torah, so that you would not turn away from me.

(﴿and giving glad tidings of a Messenger﴾) confirming him. "Mubashshiran" is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal), and its governing element is the meaning of sending. "Ilaykum" is the complement (silah) of "Rasul."

(﴿who will come after me, whose name is Ahmad﴾). Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read "min ba'dī" with a fatha on the ya'. This is the reading of al-Sulami, Zirr ibn Hubaysh and Abu Bakr from 'Asim. Abu Hatim preferred it because it is a noun, like the kaf in "min ba'dika" and the ta' in "qumta." The rest read it with sukun. It was also read as "min ba'dī ismuhu Ahmad" with the ya' dropped in pronunciation. Ahmad is the name of our Prophet ﷺ. It is a proper name transferred from an adjective, not from a verb; that adjective is the form "af'al" which is intended for comparative superlative. So the meaning of Ahmad is: the most praising of those who praise their Lord. All the prophets, may the blessings of Allah be upon them, praise Allah, and our Prophet Ahmad is the most abundant of them in praise. As for Muhammad, it is also transferred from an adjective, and it has the meaning of "praised," but it carries the sense of intensification and repetition. So "Muhammad" is one who is praised again and again, just as "al-mukarram" from generosity means one who is honoured again and again, and likewise "al-mumaddah" and similar forms. Thus the name Muhammad corresponds to its meaning, and Allah named him before he named himself with it. This is one of the signs of his prophethood, since his name is true of him. He is praised in this world for the guidance he received and the knowledge and wisdom from which he benefited others, and he is praised in the Hereafter through intercession. Thus the meaning of praise is repeated, as the wording requires. Then, he was not Muhammad until he was Ahmad: he praised his Lord, so He made him a prophet and honoured him. Therefore the name Ahmad came before the name Muhammad, and 'Isa, peace be upon him, mentioned it when he said: "His name is Ahmad." Musa, peace be upon him, also mentioned it when his Lord said to him: "That is the Ummah of Ahmad," and he said: "O Allah, make me one of the Ummah of Ahmad." So he mentioned him by Ahmad before he mentioned him by Muhammad, because his praise of his Lord came before the people's praise of him. When he was found and sent, he was Muhammad in actuality. Likewise, in intercession, he praises his Lord with the praises that Allah opens to him, so he is the most praising of people toward his Lord, then he intercedes and is praised for his intercession.

It is narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said: "My name in the Torah is Ahyad, because I drive (uhayyidu) my Ummah away from the Fire. My name in the Zabur is al-Maahi (the Eraser): Allah erases through me the worshippers of idols. My name in the Injil is Ahmad. My name in the Qur'an is Muhammad, because I am praised among the people of the heavens and the earth." And in the Sahih: "I have five names: I am Muhammad, I am Ahmad, I am al-Maahi through whom Allah erases disbelief, I am al-Haashir before whose feet people will be gathered, and I am al-'Aaqib." This has already been mentioned [see vol. 14, p. 200].

(﴿So when he came to them with clear proofs﴾) it is said: 'Isa. And it is said: Muhammad, may Allah bless them both and grant them peace.

(﴿they said, "This is clear magic."﴾) al-Kisa'i and Hamzah read "sahir" as an adjective describing the man. It is narrated that this was the reading of Ibn Mas'ud. The rest read "sihr" as an adjective describing what the Messenger brought.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 61, verse 7:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And who is more unjust﴾, meaning: there is no one more unjust (than one who invents a lie against Allah), as has been mentioned in more than one place [see vol. 6, p. 401 and vol. 7, p. 39

(And he is invited to Islam) This is an expression of wonder at those who disbelieve in Jesus and Muhammad after the miracles that appeared through them both. Talha ibn Musarrif recited (wa-huwa yuddaʿā) with a fatḥah on the yāʾ and the dāl, with shaddah on the dāl and a kasrah on the ʿayn, meaning "he claims kinship" (yantasib). Yuddaʿī and yantasib are the same.

(And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people), that is, whoever is destined by His decree to be sealed in misguidance.

The words of the Most High: (They desire to extinguish the light of Allah with their mouths). Iṭfāʾ (extinguishing) is iḫmād (quenching), and both are used of fire and of things that take its place, such as light and manifestation. Iṭfāʾ and iḫmād differ in one respect: iṭfāʾ is used for both little and much, whereas iḫmād is used only for much, not for little. One says aṭfaʾtu al-sirāj ("I extinguished the lamp") and does not say aḫmadtu al-sirāj. Regarding "the light of Allah" here there are five opinions:
First: it is the Qur'an, and they desire to nullify and deny it by speech. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn Zayd.
Second: it is Islam, and they desire to repel it with words. This was said by al-Suddi.
Third: it is Muhammad (ﷺ), and they desire his destruction through rumours. This was said by al-Ḍaḥḥak.
Fourth: it is the proofs and evidences of Allah, and they desire to nullify them through their denial and rejection. This was said by Ibn Baḥr.
Fifth: it is a parable struck, meaning: whoever wishes to extinguish the light of the sun with his mouth, finds it impossible and unattainable; likewise whoever wishes to nullify the truth. This was related by Ibn ʿIsa.

The occasion of revelation of this verse is what ʿAṭāʾ related from Ibn ʿAbbas: that the Prophet (ﷺ) was delayed in receiving revelation for forty days. Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf said: "O assembly of Jews, rejoice! Allah has extinguished the light of Muhammad in what was being sent down to him, and He was not going to complete his affair." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was saddened, so Allah the Most High revealed this verse, and revelation continued after it. Al-Mawardi, may Allah have mercy on him, related all of this.

(And Allah will perfect His light), that is, by making it manifest on the horizons. Ibn Kathir, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Ḥafṣ from ʿĀṣim recited (wa-llāhu mutimmu nūrihi) with the genitive construction (iḍāfah) on the intention of separation, like His saying: (Every soul shall taste death) [Āl ʿImrān: 185] and similar, as previously explained in Āl ʿImrān. The rest recited mutimmun nūrahu, because it refers to what is yet to come, so it acts (as a verb).

(Even though the disbelievers dislike it), from all the other categories.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 61, verse 9:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It is He who sent His Messenger with guidance﴾, i.e., Muhammad, with the truth and right guidance.

(﴿That He may make it prevail over all religion﴾), i.e., with proofs (ḥujaj). Among the meanings of prevailing (ẓuhūr) is overcoming by force in fighting. The intended meaning of prevailing is not that no other religion among the religions should remain; rather, the intended meaning is that the people of Islam should be high and dominant. Among the meanings of making it prevail is that no religion other than Islam remains at the end of time. Mujahid said: "That is when ʿĪsā (Jesus) descends; there will be no religion on earth except the religion of Islam." Abu Hurayrah said: "﴿That He may make it prevail over all religion﴾ by the coming out (of ʿĪsā). At that time no disbeliever will remain except that he embraces Islam." In Sahih Muslim, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The son of Maryam will descend as a just judge, and he will break the cross, kill the swine, abolish the jizyah, and the she-camels (al-qilāṣ [[al-qilāṣ (with a kasra on the qaf): the young she-camel.]]) will be left so that no one will pursue them, rancor, hatred and envy will vanish, and he will call people to wealth, but no one will accept it."

It was also said: "That He may make it prevail" means that He may make Muhammad (ﷺ) aware of all the religions, so that he would know them and recognize the ways of their falsehood, and what they had distorted and altered of them. "Over all religion": i.e., over the religions, because religion (dīn) is a verbal noun through which a plural is expressed.

**Fifth issue**... no, the passage begins with the first issue. Here is the translation:

There are five issues in this passage.

**The first issue:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who believe, shall I guide you to a transaction that will save you from a painful punishment?﴾ Muqatil said: It was revealed concerning Uthman ibn Maz'un, because he said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "If you permit me, I will divorce Khawlah, become a monk (tarahhabtu), have myself castrated (ikhtasaytu), forbid meat to myself, never sleep at night, and never break my fast during the day!" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Marriage is part of my Sunnah (the Prophetic way), and there is no monasticism (rahbaniyyah) in Islam. The monasticism of my community is jihad (striving) in the way of Allah, and the castration of my community is fasting. Do not forbid the good things that Allah has made lawful for you. Of my Sunnah is that I sleep and I pray at night, I break my fast and I fast. Whoever turns away from my Sunnah is not of me." Uthman said: "By Allah, I wish, O Prophet of Allah, to know which trade is most beloved to Allah, so that I may engage in it." Then this was revealed. It was also said: "adullukum" means "sa-adullukum" (I will guide you). The "trade" here is jihad, as Allah said: ﴿Indeed, Allah has purchased from the believers their lives and their properties﴾ [al-Tawbah: 111], and the verse continues. [[See vol. 8, p. 267.]] This is an address to all believers. It was also said that it is addressed to the People of the Book.

**The second issue:** His saying: (tunjikum), meaning "saves you" (takhlisukum), (min 'adhabin alim), meaning "from a painful punishment," that is, one that causes pain. This has already been discussed. [[See vol. 1, p. 198.]] The common reading is (tunjikum) with the nun sakin, from al-injaʾ (salvation). Al-Hasan and Ibn Amir, and Abu Haywah, read (tunajjikum) with a shaddah, from al-tanjiyah (deliverance).

**The third issue:** Then He explained the trade, saying: (You believe in Allah and His Messenger, and strive in the way of Allah with your wealth and your selves). He mentioned wealth first because it is the thing with which spending begins.

(That) meaning this act (is better for you) than your wealth and your lives (if you only knew). According to al-Mubarrad and al-Zajjaj, (tu'minūna) is in the sense of the imperative "Believe!" This is why (yaghfir lakum) is jussive, as an answer to the command. In the reading of Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud), it is (āminū billāh). Al-Farra said: (yaghfir lakum) is the answer to the interrogative. This is valid only if taken according to meaning: "You believe in Allah and His Messenger, and strive" is an explicative apposition (ʿatf bayān) to His saying: "shall I guide you to a transaction that will save you from a painful punishment," as if the trade had not been identified, so it was explained as belief and jihad; they are the same in meaning. It is as if he said: "Will you believe in Allah and strive? He will forgive you." Al-Zamakhshari said: The reasoning behind al-Farra's view is that the object of the guidance is the trade, and the trade is explained as belief and jihad. It is as if it were said: "Will you trade in belief and jihad? He will forgive you."

Al-Mahdawi said: If you do not interpret it this way, the question does not hold, because the sense becomes "if you are guided, He will forgive you," and forgiveness is described as being accepted through belief and not through guidance. Al-Zajjaj said: It does not follow that if He guides them to what benefits them, He will forgive them; He forgives them only when they believe and strive.

Zayd ibn Ali read (tu'minū) and (tujāhidū) with an implied imperative lam, as in the verse of the poet:

"Muhammad, let every soul be ransom for you, when you fear any calamity."

[[The speaker of this verse is disputed: some say it is Hassan, some say Abu Talib, the uncle of the Messenger (may Allah's blessings be upon him), and some say al-A'sha. (See Khizanat al-Adab, the witness of the 180th poem.) Al-Tabal means evil consequence, and has the same meaning as al-Wabal. The first half of this line appears in manuscripts H, Z, S and T in a garbled and unclear form.]]

He intended "li-tafdi" (let him ransom). Some assimilated (idgham) and said (yaghfir lakum), but the better practice is not to assimilate, because the rāʾ is a strong, repeated letter, and it is not good to assimilate it into the lām, since the stronger is not assimilated into the weaker.

**The fourth issue:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and pleasant dwellings﴾. Abu al-Husayn al-Ajurri narrated from al-Hasan who said: I asked Imran ibn Husayn and Abu Hurayrah about the interpretation of this verse, "and pleasant dwellings." They said: "You have asked the one who knows," and we asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about it, and he said: "A palace of pearl in Paradise, in which there are seventy houses of red ruby. In each house there are seventy chambers of green emerald. In each chamber there are seventy beds, and on each bed seventy couches of every color. On each couch there are seventy women of the wide-eyed houris. In each chamber there are seventy tables, and on each table seventy kinds of food. In each chamber there are seventy servants, male and female. Allah, blessed and exalted, will give the believer, in a single morning, strength enough for all of that." (It is said) "in gardens of Eden," meaning a lasting abode.

(That is the great triumph) meaning the lasting, great happiness. The origin of al-fawz (triumph) is attaining what is sought.

**The fifth issue:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and another you love﴾. Al-Farra and al-Akhfash said: "another" is coordinated with "trade," so it is in the genitive position. It was also said that its position is nominative, meaning: "and for you is another quality and another trade, which you love": (help from Allah), meaning it is help from Allah, so "help" in this case is an explanation of "another." It was also said that it is nominative as a substitute for "another," meaning: "and for you is help from Allah."

(And a near victory), meaning a spoil of war in the immediate life of this world. It was also said that it is the conquest of Makkah. Ibn Abbas said: He means the conquest of Persia and Rome.

(And give good tidings to the believers), of Allah's pleasure with them.

[[See vol. 8, p. 267.]] This is an address to all believers. It was also said that it is addressed to the People of the Book.

**The second issue:** His saying: (tunjikum), meaning "saves you" (takhlisukum), (min 'adhabin alim), meaning "from a painful punishment," that is, one that causes pain. This has already been discussed. [[See vol. 1, p. 198.]] The common reading is (tunjikum) with the nun sakin, from al-injaʾ (salvation). Al-Hasan and Ibn Amir, and Abu Haywah, read (tunajjikum) with a shaddah, from al-tanjiyah (deliverance).

**The third issue:** Then He explained the trade, saying: (You believe in Allah and His Messenger, and strive in the way of Allah with your wealth and your selves). He mentioned wealth first because it is the thing with which spending begins.

(That) meaning this act (is better for you) than your wealth and your lives (if you only knew). According to al-Mubarrad and al-Zajjaj, (tu'minūna) is in the sense of the imperative "Believe!" This is why (yaghfir lakum) is jussive, as an answer to the command. In the reading of Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud), it is (āminū billāh). Al-Farra said: (yaghfir lakum) is the answer to the interrogative. This is valid only if taken according to meaning: "You believe in Allah and His Messenger, and strive" is an explicative apposition (ʿatf bayān) to His saying: "shall I guide you to a transaction that will save you from a painful punishment," as if the trade had not been identified, so it was explained as belief and jihad; they are the same in meaning. It is as if he said: "Will you believe in Allah and strive? He will forgive you." Al-Zamakhshari said: The reasoning behind al-Farra's view is that the object of the guidance is the trade, and the trade is explained as belief and jihad. It is as if it were said: "Will you trade in belief and jihad? He will forgive you."

Al-Mahdawi said: If you do not interpret it this way, the question does not hold, because the sense becomes "if you are guided, He will forgive you," and forgiveness is described as being accepted through belief and not through guidance. Al-Zajjaj said: It does not follow that if He guides them to what benefits them, He will forgive them; He forgives them only when they believe and strive.

Zayd ibn Ali read (tu'minū) and (tujāhidū) with an implied imperative lam, as in the verse of the poet:

"Muhammad, let every soul be ransom for you, when you fear any calamity."

[[The speaker of this verse is disputed: some say it is Hassan, some say Abu Talib, the uncle of the Messenger (may Allah's blessings be upon him), and some say al-A'sha. (See Khizanat al-Adab, the witness of the 180th poem.) Al-Tabal means evil consequence, and has the same meaning as al-Wabal. The first half of this line appears in manuscripts H, Z, S and T in a garbled and unclear form.]]

He intended "li-tafdi" (let him ransom). Some assimilated (idgham) and said (yaghfir lakum), but the better practice is not to assimilate, because the rāʾ is a strong, repeated letter, and it is not good to assimilate it into the lām, since the stronger is not assimilated into the weaker.

**The fourth issue:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and pleasant dwellings﴾. Abu al-Husayn al-Ajurri narrated from al-Hasan who said: I asked Imran ibn Husayn and Abu Hurayrah about the interpretation of this verse, "and pleasant dwellings." They said: "You have asked the one who knows," and we asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about it, and he said: "A palace of pearl in Paradise, in which there are seventy houses of red ruby. In each house there are seventy chambers of green emerald. In each chamber there are seventy beds, and on each bed seventy couches of every color. On each couch there are seventy women of the wide-eyed houris. In each chamber there are seventy tables, and on each table seventy kinds of food. In each chamber there are seventy servants, male and female. Allah, blessed and exalted, will give the believer, in a single morning, strength enough for all of that." (It is said) "in gardens of Eden," meaning a lasting abode.

(That is the great triumph) meaning the lasting, great happiness. The origin of al-fawz (triumph) is attaining what is sought.

**The fifth issue:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and another you love﴾. Al-Farra and al-Akhfash said: "another" is coordinated with "trade," so it is in the genitive position. It was also said that its position is nominative, meaning: "and for you is another quality and another trade, which you love": (help from Allah), meaning it is help from Allah, so "help" in this case is an explanation of "another." It was also said that it is nominative as a substitute for "another," meaning: "and for you is help from Allah."

(And a near victory), meaning a spoil of war in the immediate life of this world. It was also said that it is the conquest of Makkah. Ibn Abbas said: He means the conquest of Persia and Rome.

(And give good tidings to the believers), of Allah's pleasure with them.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 61, verse 14:

He emphasised the command of jihad (struggle), meaning: be the disciples (ḥawāriyyūn) of your Prophet, so that Allah will make you prevail over those who oppose you, just as He made the disciples of ʿIsā prevail over those who opposed them. Ibn Kathir, Abu ʿAmr and Nafiʿ recited ﴿anṣāran lillāh﴾ with tanwin (nunation). They said: its meaning is "remain firm and be helpers of Allah with the sword against His enemies." The rest, from the people of Basra, Kufa and Syria, recited ﴿anṣāra Allāh﴾ without tanwin, dropping the lam of possession from the name of Allah, may He be exalted. Abu ʿUbayda chose this reading, citing the saying "We are the helpers of Allah" (without tanwin), and its meaning is "be helpers of the religion of Allah." Then it was said: there is an implied element in the speech, that is, "Say to them, O Muhammad: be the helpers of Allah." It was also said: this is the beginning of an address from Allah, that is, "Be helpers as the companions of ʿIsā did, and by the praise of Allah they were helpers and they were disciples." The ḥawāriyyūn (disciples; the word means the chosen companions of the messengers) — Maʿmar said: that was by the praise of Allah, that is, they supported Him, and they were seventy men, and they are the ones who pledged allegiance to him on the night of al-ʿAqaba. It was also said: they were from Quraysh. Qatada named them: Abu Bakr, ʿUmar, ʿAli, Talha, al-Zubayr, Saʿd ibn Malik, Abu ʿUbayda (whose name was ʿĀmir), ʿUthman ibn Madhʿun and Hamza ibn ʿAbd al-Muttalib; he did not mention Saʿid among them, and he mentioned Jaʿfar ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with them all.

(As ʿIsā ibn Maryam said to the ḥawāriyyūn) They were his chosen ones, twelve men, and their names have already passed in Surat Āl ʿImrān [[See vol. 4, p. 97; it should be noted that their names were not mentioned there, but rather the reason for their being named.]]. They were the first of the Children of Israel to believe in him, as said by Ibn ʿAbbas. Muqatil said: Allah said to ʿIsā, "When you enter the town, go to the river on which the qassārūn are [[al-qaṣṣār: the one who launders and whitens clothes; see vol. 4, p. 97 and p. 100]], and ask them for support." So ʿIsā came to them and said, "Who will be my helpers in the way of Allah?" They said, "We will support you." So they believed him and supported him. The meaning of "Who are my helpers towards Allah" is "who are my helpers along with Allah," just as you say: "al-dhawd ila al-dhawd ibil" (meaning: a group together with a group are camels), that is, "together with the group." It was also said: that is, "who are my helpers in what brings one closer to Allah." This has already been discussed in Āl ʿImrān. (Then a group of the Children of Israel believed, and a group disbelieved.) The two groups in the time of ʿIsā separated after his being raised up to heaven, as was explained earlier in Āl ʿImrān. So We strengthened those who believed against their enemies, who disbelieved in ʿIsā. Then they became dominant, that is, victorious. Ibn ʿAbbas said: Allah strengthened those who believed in the time of ʿIsā by the manifestation of Muhammad (ﷺ) over the religion of the disbelievers. Mujahid said: they were strengthened in their time over those who disbelieved in ʿIsā. It was also said: We now strengthen the Muslims against the two misguided sects: the one that said He was God and was raised up, and the one that said He was the son of Allah, so Allah raised him to Himself, because ʿIsā ibn Maryam never fought anyone and there was no fighting in the religion of his companions after him. Zayd ibn ʿAli and Qatada said: "Then they became dominant" means victorious through proof and evidence, for they said, as is reported: "Do you not know that ʿIsā used to sleep while Allah does not sleep, and that ʿIsā used to eat while Allah, exalted is He, does not eat?" It was also said: this verse was revealed concerning the messengers of ʿIsā, peace be upon him. Ibn Ishaq said: those whom ʿIsā sent from the disciples and followers were Tuwtrus and Bulus to Rome; Andarayas and Mathi to the land whose people eat people; Tumas to the land of Babil in the East; Filibus to Qartajanna, which is Ifriqiya; Yuhannas to Daqsus, the village of the People of the Cave; Yaʿqubus to Urishlim, which is Bayt al-Maqdis; Ibn Tulima to al-ʿUrabiyya, which is the land of the Hijaz; Simun to the land of the Berbers; and Yahuda and Birdas to Alexandria and its surroundings [[It should be noted that these names appear distorted in the copies of the original; we have kept them as they appear in the History of al-Tabari (vol. 3, part 1, p. 737, Europe edition).]]. So Allah strengthened them with proof. Then they became dominant, that is, high, from your saying: "I ascended (ẓahartu) upon the wall," meaning I climbed upon it. And Allah, glorified and exalted is He, knows best what is correct, and to Him is the return and the final place.
